front-page canonical Best Practice Advice statements

atoms.canonical_statement: The AGA Clinical Practice Update aims to provide practical, evidence-based best-practice advice for clinicians managing adult Clostridioides difficile infection.
The expert review was commissioned by the AGA Institute Clinical Practice Updates Committee and AGA Governing Board to provide timely guidance on CDI management.
The review was developed from expert opinion and a review of the published literature.
Systematic reviews were not performed for this Clinical Practice Update.
The best-practice advice statements do not carry formal ratings for evidence quality or strength because systematic reviews were not performed.
CDI prevention in health care settings should include proper barrier protection and disinfection with U.S. EPA-approved sporicidal agents.
Patients with CDI should be counseled to wash hands and consider disinfecting home areas potentially contaminated with C. difficile spores to reduce reinfection.
Patients should be reassured that transmission of CDI to unaffected family members is uncommon.
CDI is a clinical diagnosis requiring compatible symptoms, typically acute diarrhea after antibiotics, together with supportive laboratory testing.
Multistep CDI testing is preferred for diagnostic accuracy.
Patients with discordant CDI testing should be treated when clinical suspicion remains high.
Hospitalized patients with CDI should be classified at diagnosis as nonsevere, severe, or fulminant.
White blood cell count greater than 15,000 cells/µL and/or creatinine greater than 1.5 times baseline indicate severe CDI and higher risk for recurrence and poor outcomes.
Shock, ileus, or megacolon in a patient with CDI identifies fulminant disease.
Fidaxomicin 200 mg orally twice daily for 10 days is favored as first-line therapy for nonfulminant CDI because of its narrower spectrum and lower recurrence rates.
Oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days is an acceptable alternative for nonfulminant CDI.
Metronidazole should not be used for CDI outside fulminant disease.
When oral vancomycin is prescribed four times daily for CDI, doses may be given during waking hours; patients do not need to wake overnight to take it exactly every 6 hours.
The cited Cochrane review found fidaxomicin more effective than vancomycin for symptomatic cure without recurrence at 1 month (RR 1.17, 95% CI 1.07–1.27; 71% vs 61%).

population.label: Adults with C. difficile-associated diarrhoea included in the cited Cochrane review

quantitative_result.original_result_text: 71% cure with fidaxomicin compared with 61% with vancomycin; relative risk, 1.17; 95% confidence interval, 1.07–1.27

atoms.canonical_statement: Cholestyramine and other bile acid-binding agents should not be used as CDI monotherapy or concurrently with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin.
Psyllium fiber can be used to bulk stools after recovery from CDI.
Routine test of cure should not be performed after CDI treatment.
Stool testing after CDI treatment should be reserved for persistent or worsening diarrheal symptoms.

Antimotility agents are contraindicated in untreated CDI, fulminant CDI, and severe colonic inflammatory bowel disease; if loperamide is used, it should be for the shortest duration and only after anti-CDI therapy has begun.
A first CDI recurrence within 8 weeks of completing anti-CDI therapy should be treated with either a tapering course of vancomycin or fidaxomicin.
CDI treatment should include assessment of recurrence risk and consideration of microbiota restoration therapy to prevent further recurrence.

After initial fidaxomicin, a first recurrence can be treated with a vancomycin taper/pulse regimen or extended-pulsed fidaxomicin 200 mg twice daily on days 1–5, then once daily on alternate days on days 7–25.
After initial vancomycin, a first recurrence should be treated with fidaxomicin 200 mg twice daily for 10 days or the extended-pulsed fidaxomicin regimen.
Vancomycin taper/pulse regimens extending beyond 60 days have not been studied and are not likely to provide additional benefit.
Fecal microbiota-based therapy should be offered after treatment of a second recurrence, corresponding to the third CDI episode.

Microbiota restoration therapy may be considered after an initial CDI episode or first recurrence when risk for further recurrence is high or the initial episode was particularly morbid or difficult to treat.
Anti-CDI antibacterial therapy should generally be stopped 1–4 days before microbiota restoration therapy.

In severely immunocompromised patients, the AGA guideline recommendation summarized by the authors favors deferring fecal microbiota-based therapies and continuing antibiotic therapy until the severe immunocompromised state resolves.

Long-term low-dose suppressive oral vancomycin 125 mg daily may be considered for secondary prophylaxis in selected patients with multiple recurrent CDI who cannot receive microbiota-based therapy, have failed it, or have ongoing conditions that make recurrence difficult to prevent.
Some selected patients may require ongoing suppressive oral vancomycin because recurrence risk remains high after prophylaxis is stopped.
The review reports that recurrent CDI exceeds 30% after discontinuation of suppressive oral vancomycin.

population.label: Patients with multiply recurrent CDI receiving prolonged oral vancomycin in the cited evidence

concept.text: Discontinuation of prolonged low-dose oral vancomycin

quantitative_result.effect_measure: reported recurrence rate lower bound percent
quantitative_result.original_result_text: the likelihood of recurrent CDI exceeds 30% following discontinuation of vancomycin prophylaxis

atoms.canonical_statement: The cited prospective study found no detectable serum vancomycin in 98% of patients receiving oral vancomycin, including patients with renal insufficiency.

population.label: Patients with C. difficile infection in the cited prospective oral-vancomycin absorption study

quantitative_result.effect_measure: percent with no detectable serum concentration
quantitative_result.original_result_text: oral vancomycin produced no detectable serum levels in 98% of patients

atoms.canonical_statement: Fulminant CDI should be managed by a multidisciplinary team including gastroenterology or infectious disease, surgery, and medicine or critical care.
Fulminant CDI should initially be treated with vancomycin 500 mg orally or enterally every 6 hours plus metronidazole 500 mg intravenously every 8 hours.
Rectal vancomycin 500 mg every 6 hours should be added to fulminant CDI therapy when ileus is present.
Patients with fulminant CDI who have not improved or who worsen after 48 hours of aggressive medical therapy should be considered for fecal microbiota transplantation or colectomy.

After clinical response in fulminant CDI, typically after 3–5 days, therapy can be narrowed to vancomycin 125 mg four times daily; treatment should last at least 10 days, and the authors favor 14 days.
Multidose conventional fecal microbiota transplantation from fresh directed donors or institutional stool banks, delivered by lower endoscopy, should be considered for fulminant CDI.
Fecal microbiota live-jslm and fecal microbiota spores live-brpk have not been studied and are not approved for treatment of severe or fulminant CDI.
Patients recovering from severe or fulminant CDI should remain on suppressive vancomycin until a final outpatient fecal microbiota transplantation can be administered.
No randomized controlled trials exist for fecal microbiota transplantation as treatment for fulminant CDI; the recommendation relies on observational evidence.

Across 5 observational studies including 647 patients with severe or fulminant CDI, conventional FMT was associated with lower mortality than standard care (RR 0.37, 95% CI 0.23–0.59), with a reported number needed to treat of 4.

population.label: Adults hospitalized with severe or fulminant CDI in 5 observational studies

quantitative_result.original_result_text: relative risk, 0.37; 95% confidence interval, 0.23–0.59; number needed to treat of 4

atoms.canonical_statement: Most patients treated with conventional FMT for severe or fulminant CDI are expected to need 2–3 administrations of liquid FMT via lower endoscopy to resolve the acute infection.
FMT is not advised for severe or fulminant CDI when bowel perforation or obstruction or high-grade colonic stricture is present.
Oral vancomycin is not advised during systemic antibiotic administration solely to prevent CDI.
Probiotics are not advised to prevent either an initial or recurrent CDI episode.
Patients should be encouraged to consume a healthy diet with varied fruits and vegetables and both soluble and insoluble fiber to support restoration of healthy gut microbiota.

The only randomized trial cited for oral vancomycin prophylaxis found a 13.5 percentage-point absolute reduction in recurrent CDI that was not statistically significant, and the trial was not powered to detect that difference.

population.label: Participants in the cited randomized trial of oral vancomycin prophylaxis for recurrent CDI prevention

quantitative_result.original_result_text: OVP was associated with a 13.5% absolute reduction in CDI; the study was not powered to detect that difference

atoms.canonical_statement: Evidence for oral vancomycin prophylaxis during systemic antibiotic exposure is limited and conflicting; the cited randomized trial was underpowered for the observed difference.
Use of proton pump inhibitors should be evaluated during CDI treatment and efforts to prevent recurrence.
A proton pump inhibitor does not need to be discontinued when a legitimate indication exists.
When no clear PPI indication exists, cessation should be discussed; there is no evidence supporting dose reduction as an alternative strategy.
Pooled observational data cited in the review reported recurrent CDI in 24% of PPI users versus 18% of nonusers.

population.label: Patients in pooled observational studies of PPI exposure and recurrent CDI

quantitative_result.effect_measure: recurrent CDI rate among PPI users percent
quantitative_result.original_result_text: 24% in PPI users vs 18% in nonusers

atoms.canonical_statement: The largest randomized trial cited by the review included more than 17,000 participants followed for 3 years and reported 11 CDI cases among PPI users versus 4 among nonusers, with a number needed to harm of 1800 for daily pantoprazole.

population.label: More than 17,000 participants in the cited randomized trial

quantitative_result.original_result_text: 11 cases among PPI users vs 4 cases in nonusers; number needed to harm = 1800 with daily pantoprazole

atoms.canonical_statement: Patients with a history of CDI should be specifically counseled to avoid unnecessary antibiotic therapy.
Patients with prior CDI should still receive antibiotics when there is an appropriate indication and should not be counseled to fear necessary antibiotic use.

The authors disclose industry advisory, consulting, teaching, personal-income, and OpenBiome-related relationships for Monika Fischer, Colleen R. Kelly, and Byron P. Vaughn; Anne F. Peery reports no conflict in the article disclosure.

schema_gaps: The LiteratureAtom schema has no dedicated guideline_recommendation or best_practice_advice atom kind. AGA Best Practice Advice statements are represented as author_conclusion atoms with descriptive tags.

This source is an expert review/clinical practice update rather than primary literature. Quantitative evidence summarized from cited studies is tagged secondary_reported_result and remains anchored to this review rather than being represented as primary-study evidence.
extraction_limitations: The article-referenced Patient Cleaning Guide and Supplementary Table 1 were not provided with the uploaded PDF and were not silently obtained from outside sources.
Bibliography entries were extracted separately to Markdown and were not atomized as evidence.
Regulatory status, product availability, and guideline currency claims were summarized as reported in the 2026 source and were not externally verified in this run.
Reference 13 appears internally mismatched to the Table 1 statement that cites it; this was preserved as a source-integrity issue rather than corrected.
